newsitem.title: UK: UK beet crop sees early diseases but no threat.
newsitem.headline: UK beet crop sees early diseases but no threat.

text.p: Britain's sugar beet crop has started to suffer from an early emergence of field diseases which farmers should still be able to control by harvest time, beet experts said on Friday.
In a recent bulletin, the industry-funded IACR-Broom's Barn research centre said powdery mildew had been found in several fields in the counties of Suffolk and Norfolk, but only on a few plants.
A few plants were also showing severe symptoms of nitrogen deficiency, apparently related to poor rooting.
"There is nothing there that is threatening what we believe to be quite a good crop," said a spokeswoman at the National Farmers Union (NFU).
"Hopefully powdery mildew will be able to be controlled, measures can be taken to offset the effects so that there's no national effect from those diseases."
Experts said the mildew, which appears as a grey mould starting from the outer leaves, had emerged earlier than expected as it was usually a problem in August.
"The incidence of powdery mildew is earlier than usual. I think it's something to watch out for...but I'm not suggesting there's going to be an epidemic," said an official at Broom's Barn.
Black aphid colonies were dying out after mantaining a heavy presence which had been effectively controlled by plant predators and other parasites.
Lack of rainfall could be another problem despite ample precipitation during June, possibly leading to wilting and a loss in sugar yields.
Much of last month's moisture was held in top layers of soil, the Broom's Barn bulletin said.
"There's still three months to play which will need moisture as we go forward but at the moment we're okay in terms of beet," the NFU spokeswoman said.
Sugar contents were likely to be lower than last year, mainly because the levels seen from the 1996/97 crop were extremely high, she said.
British Sugar's eighth and last field test for last year's crop, conducted on September 23, showed sugar content at 17.84 percent compared with 15.80 at the same stage in 1995/96.
This year's first field dig is scheduled for the first week of August.
"It's unlikely we'll see similar sugar contents to last year, because that really was exceptional, so I would expect them to be down," the NFU spokeswoman said.

British Sugar plc, the sugar arm of Associated British Foods said this year's beet crop was currently enjoying ideal growing conditions with the national outlook was good despite localised setbacks. --London Newsroom +44 171 542 8064
